1.pericope_label: In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon Daniel had a dream... I saw in my vision by night, and, behold, the four winds of the heaven strove upon the great sea. And four great beasts came up from the sea
debates: Whether the great sea is the Mediterranean or the heathen world
What error in the returning exiles the vision was given to correct
Why empires are figured as beasts rather than as men
outliers: Ellicott passes on Jerome’s note that these dreams carried no weight outside Israel
Calvin says kingdoms are beautiful in themselves and that the tyranny is the ruler’s own
Keil and Delitzsch cites winged figures found at Babylon as bearing on the book’s date
themes: Seventy years counted out just as new storms are promised
Winds meeting from every quarter at once
A dream written down lest it pass away
Empires described as the greatest robberies

4.pericope_label: The first was like a lion, and had eagle’s wings... another beast, a second, like to a bear... another, like a leopard, which had upon the back of it four wings of a fowl
debates: What the raising of the bear on one side signifies
What the three ribs in its mouth stand for
Whether the plucked wings refer to the king or to the kingdom
outliers: Clarke derives the whole science of heraldry from these symbols and the Egyptian hieroglyphics
Ellicott refuses to fix the reference for want of historical detail
Calvin says Alexander would have been intoxicated by ambition had he never tasted wine
themes: A winged lion still visible in ruined stonework
A world growing steadily worse from one empire to the next
A people hidden among mountains until one man named them
Conquest from one sea to another inside twelve years

7.pericope_label: After this I saw in the night visions, and behold a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible... and it had ten horns. I considered the horns, and, behold, there came up among them another little horn
debates: Whether the little horn is the papacy, the Turk, the Caesars, or a Syrian king
How far forward in history the vision is meant to reach
Why the fourth beast is given no animal name
outliers: Calvin rejects both the papal and the Turkish readings and stops the vision at the first advent
Keil and Delitzsch asks why the eyes are specifically a man’s when the horn is already a man
Calvin says the Jews adopt their reading because they cannot otherwise find their Christ
themes: A monster no animal is fierce enough to picture
A conqueror content with fame beside masters who kept what they took
Ten horns counted off against ten toes
A horn with eyes that watches the others

9.pericope_label: I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit... A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him: thousand thousands ministered unto him... the judgment was set, and the books were opened
debates: Whether the thrones are cast down or set up
Who sits on the seats beside the judge
Whether the scene is the last judgment or the fall of the fourth kingdom
outliers: Ellicott rejects the derivation of the title from Babylonian mythology as inconceivable
Clarke notes this as the only place in scripture where the Father appears in human form
Calvin says God shows something terrible whenever he appears, to excite fear and not merely wonder
themes: Seats set out in a semicircle for an assize
Armies that need no mustering
A river of fire that cannot be stopped
Books kept in an unfailing memory

11.pericope_label: I beheld then because of the voice of the great words which the horn spake: I beheld even till the beast was slain, and his body destroyed, and given to the burning flame
debates: Why the beast rather than the horn is the thing destroyed
When the fourth empire can be said to have been slain
Whether the clause about the other beasts follows in time or looks back
outliers: Clarke reports that no kingdom succeeds this one, which is why its body is destroyed and not merely its rule
Calvin dates the end of the empire from the point when no Roman held it
Calvin explains the disorder by a Hebrew habit of returning to what was omitted
themes: A judgment brought on by words rather than deeds
A title carried off while the city stayed enslaved
A swineherd made emperor by the soldiers
Trials long enough to weary those who endure them

13.pericope_label: I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days... And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom
debates: Why the figure is only like a son of man
Whether the giving of the kingdom begins the reign or closes it
What the coming to the Ancient of days answers to
outliers: Ellicott argues from the single word serve that the figure is spoken of as God
Calvin says the likeness is used because the flesh was not yet assumed, not because it was unreal
Calvin refuses to carry the giving of the kingdom forward to the end of all things
themes: A second act following the destruction of the first
A word wrested by those who denied a real body
A distance closed by someone standing in our own nature
Worship named by a verb reserved for God

15.pericope_label: I Daniel was grieved in my spirit in the midst of my body... These great beasts, which are four, are four kings, which shall arise out of the earth. But the saints of the most High shall take the kingdom
debates: Whether kings or kingdoms are meant by the four
How a term of a few centuries can be called for ever and ever
Whose saints are meant in the promise
outliers: Clarke builds an argument for the soul’s separate subsistence out of the word for sheath
Keil and Delitzsch reports a dating argument drawn from the tense of one verb
Calvin measures the everlasting by the impatience of those who wait
themes: A body treated as the scabbard of a weapon
A prophet fainting from what he was shown, not from fear
Exile reckoned as equivalent to the tomb
Three months of trouble and men already arguing with God

19.pericope_label: Then I would know the truth of the fourth beast... I beheld, and the same horn made war with the saints, and prevailed against them; until the Ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the most High
debates: Whether the horn that makes war is Antiochus, the Caesars, or the papacy
Whether the brazen claws belong to the original description
Whether judgment is given to the saints or executed for them
outliers: Calvin rejects the Antiochus reading on the ground that Antiochus was not singular enough
Keil and Delitzsch refuses to let the saints be made the judges
Calvin reads the eyes and the mouth off against the manners of the early Caesars
themes: A claw that appears only when the vision is retold
A few robbers on a desert spot ending as masters of a sea
Rulers sitting low in the seats of tribunes
God described as asleep until he acts

23.pericope_label: The fourth beast shall be the fourth kingdom upon earth... And he shall speak great words against the most High, and shall wear out the saints of the most High, and think to change times and laws
debates: Whether the ten kings are successive or contemporary
Whether the great words are doctrine or imperial edicts
How the time and times and dividing of time are to be counted
outliers: Ellicott says no account of the ten horns has proved satisfactory and counsels patience
Calvin calls Rome neither a republic nor a kingdom but a confused compound
Calvin denies that the great words mean teaching at all
themes: Wars celebrated by the people who fought them and by nobody else
A government that was never once settled
A triumvir left alive because he held a priesthood
Institutions the horn only thinks to change

26.pericope_label: But the judgment shall sit, and they shall take away his dominion... And the kingdom and dominion, and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven, shall be given to the people of the saints of the most High
debates: At what point the fourth beast can be said to have been slain
Whether the promise has been accomplished or waits for the last day
What the matter is that Daniel kept in his heart
outliers: Calvin says almost all Christian interpreters read this of the last advent and that all of them are wrong
Calvin dates the death of the empire from the day low-born foreigners governed it
Clarke applies the prophet’s trouble of mind to his own conjectures
themes: A court described only by what it takes away
Noble senators replaced by the meanest of men as an insult
A curiosity that asks why God stopped where he did
A vision kept in the heart rather than published
